concepts.title: Mathematically Acceptable Statements
concepts.definition: A mathematical statement is a declarative sentence that lands firmly on exactly one truth side: it is certainly true or certainly false, never both and never undecided. Questions, orders, exclamations and sentences with an undetermined variable do not qualify.
concepts.key_idea: Acceptable statement means the counter is exactly 1: precisely one of the two truth labels applies.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.2, examples 'two plus two equals four', 'x plus 1 equals 5', 'February has 30 days'

solution_steps.action: check the sentence declares something rather than asking, ordering or exclaiming
solution_steps.explain: only declarative sentences can carry a truth value

solution_steps.action: test whether the truth is fixed with no free variable left
solution_steps.explain: an open sentence such as x plus 1 equals 5 stays undecided until x is chosen

solution_steps.action: confirm exactly one of true or false holds, then report that side
solution_steps.explain: a sentence that is both, neither, or sometimes-true fails to be a statement

concepts.title: Truth Value of the And Connective
concepts.definition: The compound 'p and q' behaves like a series circuit: it comes out true only in the single case where both component statements are true, and false whenever either component fails.
concepts.key_idea: Encode true as 1 and false as 0; multiplying the two values leaves 1 only when both are 1.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.3, the use of AND: true exactly when both parts are true

solution_steps.action: encode each part as 1 for true and 0 for false

concepts.title: Truth Value of the Inclusive Or
concepts.definition: The compound 'p or q' is satisfied when at least one part holds, including the case where both hold at once. In truth arithmetic the double-counted both-true corner is subtracted back out.
concepts.key_idea: Add the two truth values, then remove the overlap so the both-true case does not exceed 1.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.3, the use of OR: true when at least one part is true (inclusive or)

solution_steps.action: measure the both-true overlap
solution_steps.explain: the product is 1 only when p and q are simultaneously true

solution_steps.action: add the parts and drop the double count
solution_steps.explain: this is the inclusion-exclusion form of the inclusive or

concepts.title: Negation with the Not Connective
concepts.definition: Negation flips a truth value to the opposite one: the negation of a true statement is false and of a false statement is true. In the 1 and 0 encoding the flip is one minus the value.
concepts.key_idea: Not is the mirror: subtract the truth value from 1.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.3, the use of NOT: reverses the truth value of p

solution_steps.action: flip the truth value
solution_steps.explain: one minus the value swaps 1 with 0

concepts.title: If-Then Implication Truth Value
concepts.definition: The implication 'if p then q' fails in one case only: a true antecedent followed by a false consequent. Whenever p is already false the promise is broken by nothing and the implication counts as vacuously true.
concepts.key_idea: Only true-then-false scores 0; every other row, including false antecedents, scores 1.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.3, if p then q: false antecedent makes the implication vacuously true

solution_steps.action: record whether the antecedent fails

concepts.title: If and Only If as Matching Truth Values
concepts.definition: The biconditional 'p if and only if q' insists the two parts carry the same truth value on both sides, which makes q both the necessary and the sufficient condition for p. It scores 1 on the two agreeing rows and 0 on the two disagreeing rows.
concepts.key_idea: Agreement is 1 minus the gap; equal values give 1, different values give 0.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.3, p if and only if q: both parts carry the same truth value

solution_steps.action: measure the disagreement gap
solution_steps.explain: the absolute difference is 1 exactly when the two sides disagree

solution_steps.action: convert agreement into a truth value
solution_steps.explain: one minus the gap is 1 when the values match and 0 when they clash

concepts.title: Converse, Inverse and Contrapositive
concepts.definition: From 'if p then q' three cousins are built by shuffling and negating: the converse swaps the parts, the inverse negates both, and the contrapositive both swaps and negates. The contrapositive always agrees with the original implication in every row; the converse and inverse are free to disagree.
concepts.key_idea: Swap plus negate gives the contrapositive, the only cousin guaranteed to share the original truth table.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.4, converse if q then p, inverse if not p then not q, contrapositive if not q then not p

solution_steps.action: swap the two parts to build the converse
solution_steps.explain: converse reads if q then p and needs its own proof of truth

solution_steps.action: negate both parts without swapping for the inverse
solution_steps.explain: inverse reads if not p then not q

solution_steps.action: swap and negate together for the contrapositive
solution_steps.explain: if not q then not p must match the original implication row by row

concepts.title: Quantifiers: For All and There Exists
concepts.definition: A quantifier says how much of the domain a predicate covers: the universal quantifier claims every element satisfies it, the existential claims at least one does. Negating swaps the two kinds and negates the predicate itself.
concepts.key_idea: Not pushes 'for all' to 'there exists not' and 'there exists' to 'for all not'.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.3, universal quantifier for all and existential quantifier there exists, negating one yields the other

solution_steps.action: negate by swapping the quantifier and negating the predicate
solution_steps.explain: the negation of every is some counterexample; the negation of some is a universal failure

solution_steps.action: test the claim against the domain: a universal dies by one exception, an existential lives by one instance

concepts.title: Syllogism Validity
concepts.definition: A syllogism is a three-line deductive argument: a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion that must follow of necessity. The conclusion is accepted only when every situation satisfying both premises also satisfies it.
concepts.key_idea: Check every case the premises allow; one allowed case breaking the conclusion kills the argument.

solution_steps.action: separate the major premise, the minor premise and the proposed conclusion

solution_steps.explain: validity looks only inside the world the premises create

solution_steps.action: accept the conclusion only if no such case breaks it
solution_steps.explain: a single permitted counterexample marks the syllogism invalid

concepts.title: Classification: Odd One Out
concepts.definition: Classification puzzles list items where all but one share a property; the task is to name the outsider together with the property the rest obey. The rule must be stated, not just the item picked.
concepts.key_idea: Find what the group has in common; the item missing it is the answer.

solution_steps.action: state the rule and the outsider together
solution_steps.explain: an answer without the shared property is incomplete

concepts.title: Coding-Decoding by Letter Shift
concepts.definition: In a shift code each letter is moved a fixed number of steps along the alphabet. Comparing one known plain word with its coded form reveals the shift, and the same shift then encodes or decodes any other word, wrapping around at the ends of the alphabet.
concepts.key_idea: One known pair fixes the shift; wrap positions with mod 26 so Z joins hands with A.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_007_math_logical_reasoning.txt, section 7.5, coding-decoding: a word is encoded by a letter-shift or positional rule
